title: Cities: Skylines | Power, Politics, & Planning: Episode 1: Parking
premise: The presenter uses three increasingly destructive Cities: Skylines parking builds to argue that generous municipal parking minimums consume land, displace neighbors, raise development costs, and create politically persistent parking complaints despite abundant off-street supply.
coverage: Three parking builds progress from a huge suburban office lot to garages and surface lots that displace neighboring homes and businesses. Real-city photographs, Shoup’s book and a Black Friday parking tweet extend the argument. Policy claims and displacement estimates belong to the presenter.

panels.heading: Opening identity and disproportionate parking
panels.description: A white title card displays the series name, blue Cities: Skylines bird, and ep. 1: PARKING, following aerial views of the office and its huge lot.
panels.camera: Several aerial angles around the lot give way to a static title graphic.
panels.action: Static title graphic; no visible character action.
panels.notes: The introduction is credited to Brahms’s Tragic Overture, Op. 81, performed by the Musopen Symphony.

panels.heading: Franklin gives way to a modern planning series
panels.description: The office faces a broad divided road; PARKING appears in white over the game view as the presenter promises realistic lots and explains why they are dumb.
panels.camera: Largely fixed elevated frontal view, with moving road traffic.
panels.action: The game city remains running beneath the topic label.
panels.visualGag: The ordinary-looking office tutorial sets up the episode’s irony: realistic parking takes far more land than the building it serves.

panels.heading: Rule of thumb—not a real-life recommendation
panels.description: Black card: RULE OF THUMB (FOR CITIES: SKYLINES, NOT REAL LIFE), x amount parking per unit of floor area, .75 < x < 2.
panels.camera: Static card with successive text additions.
panels.action: On-screen formula builds up; no human action.
panels.notes: The explicit visual qualification prevents mistaking the game heuristic for a recommended real-world regulation.

panels.heading: Case 1: cubicle farm on a greenfield site
panels.description: CASE 1: SUBURBAN OFFICE labels a lone dark office tower beside roads and vacant green land.
panels.camera: Several elevated angles around the office.
panels.action: No demolition yet; building and open site establish the demonstration.
panels.visualGag: The cubicle-farm and spreadsheet-mine jokes introduce a modest office footprint that will be dwarfed by its parking lot.

panels.heading: Measuring with whole office buildings
panels.description: Identical office copies fill a rectangular bank of roofs next to the original building, with a selected copy highlighted blue.
panels.camera: The office copies are shown from increasingly overhead angles.
panels.action: Game editing duplicates the building to measure cumulative floor area.
panels.visualGag: Whole office buildings become rulers for the much larger parking footprint. Once the copies disappear, the empty lot shows how much land the cars need.

panels.heading: Delete the measuring buildings
panels.description: One office survives while an enormous path outline and demolition dust replace the bank of copies.
panels.camera: Changing overhead angles; a pale tool or traffic overlay alternates with the normal game view.
panels.action: The copies are bulldozed; paths preserve their collective footprint.
panels.visualGag: The extravagant bank of office buildings disappears so that the same land can be reserved for cars.

panels.heading: Asphalt and parking rows consume the outline
panels.description: Long rows of white parking lines are selected on the dark paved lot.
panels.camera: Wide overhead site views give way to close views of the parking rows.
panels.action: The editor lays pavement and repeated parking-space assets.
panels.visualGag: The land measured with multiple towers becomes rows of spaces for storing cars.

panels.heading: Accessible spaces are not optional
panels.description: Three blue wheelchair-marked spaces with striped access aisles sit along the lot edge.
panels.camera: Close overhead views of regular rows and accessible spaces.
panels.action: Accessible-space assets are placed.
panels.visualGag: The accessible stalls accompany the presenter’s mock threat to find out if viewers omit them. The accessibility appeal is sincere.
panels.notes: No disabled person or simulated inability to enter is shown; that is the narration’s hypothetical.

panels.heading: The lot gets landscaped
panels.description: Trees and planted islands appear near the office and arterial, with the brush and asset menus visible.
panels.camera: Changing close oblique and overhead angles.
panels.action: The editor places trees and roadside details.
panels.visualGag: Trees and planted islands dress up the enormous paved site before the narrator imagines an office worker’s miserable lunch break.

panels.heading: Sad benches and the tuna-salad lunch
panels.description: Repeated empty dark benches line a paved path among trees; the prop menu is searched for bench.
panels.camera: Close path views alternate with a wider view, then return to the benches.
panels.action: Bench props are placed; no seated worker is visible.
panels.visualGag: The empty benches provide a setting for the narrator’s sad-lunch fantasy. The boss, sandwich, and personal insults exist only in speech.
panels.notes: The imagined lunch and boss scene continues over the detailing.

panels.heading: Back to harmless-looking flowers
panels.description: Small flowering plants and a fountain occupy the office frontage after the bench placement.
panels.camera: Close overhead planting view, then a wider frontal view.
panels.action: The editor places a red-flowering tree/plant near the fountain.
panels.visualGag: After the narrated workplace nightmare, the tutorial blandly returns to planting flowers.
panels.notes: The translucent rectangle is a flower-tree tooltip.

panels.heading: Huge finished lot—and still too little parking
panels.description: A UI-free aerial view shows the completed almost-empty lot dwarfing its office building.
panels.camera: Façade close-ups and wider aerial angles around the office and lot.
panels.action: Road traffic passes the completed office and lot.
panels.visualGag: The landscaped sea of stalls looks excessive, yet the presenter says 244 spaces barely cover an implausibly small office population.

panels.heading: Case 2: a rehab inside an existing neighborhood
panels.description: CASE 2: LARGE REHAB appears over a warehouse-sized building amid continuous rows of homes and storefronts.
panels.camera: Cut from the office to elevated angles around the warehouse rehab.
panels.action: Existing buildings establish what the coming garage will displace.
panels.visualGag: Unlike the greenfield office site, the rehab is surrounded by occupied buildings. The coming garage will displace its neighbors.

panels.heading: A garage solves the arithmetic
panels.description: An isolated parking structure is shown with 4 x 7 x 4 = 112, exceeding the rehab’s narrated 84-block need.
panels.camera: Open-land view, then closer elevated angles around the garage.
panels.action: Garage and its access road are placed and examined.
panels.visualGag: The vertical parking solution looks efficient until it is placed in the neighborhood.

panels.heading: Searching for the least destructive placement
panels.description: A blue ghost parking garage is trial-positioned over buildings beside the rehab.
panels.camera: Back in the neighborhood, the editor switches between top-down angles.
panels.action: The editor moves the garage preview through occupied parcels.
panels.visualGag: Searching for the least destructive position still puts the garage on top of neighboring buildings.

panels.heading: Six houses and six apartments disappear
panels.description: Cleared ground opens beside the rehab; white captions list 6 ROWHOUSES and 6 SMALL APARTMENT BUILDINGS.
panels.camera: Changing elevated angles around the garage footprint.
panels.action: Buildings are bulldozed; dust and warning markers mark the clearing.
panels.visualGag: The demolition tally gives the sarcastic parking-for-everyone claim its human cost. The next panel’s smiling game feedback makes the contradiction worse.

panels.heading: Displacement earns smiling game feedback
panels.description: The placed garage fills the gap; captions add 6 BUSINESSES & 20-30 FAMILIES, while bright green smiling icons appear across surrounding buildings.
panels.camera: Rapid angle changes and wider views, then a cut to storefronts.
panels.action: The garage is committed and neighborhood feedback icons pop up.
panels.visualGag: Green smiles celebrate the garage beside a tally of destroyed homes, shops, and displaced families. The narration calls it worth it.
panels.notes: The smiles are game feedback, not displaced residents’ reactions.

panels.heading: A win-win for everyone except the losers
panels.description: Beauty views show storefronts, the rehab, and its adjoining new garage amid remaining row houses.
panels.camera: Low storefront views, then changing angles and a pullback around the rehab.
panels.action: Completed neighborhood showcase; vehicle positions change.
panels.visualGag: Respectable views of the finished rehab accompany the sarcastic win-win claim and the account of ruined livelihoods. The game’s green smiles belong to the same destructive project.
panels.notes: The narrator mentions dumpster space. Later detailing shows bins and debris beside the garage.

panels.heading: Case 3: the small hotel rehab
panels.description: CASE 3: SMALL REHAB labels a narrow corner building with exterior fire escapes and a roof sign in a dense block.
panels.camera: Cut to the corner site, shown from several elevated angles.
panels.action: Existing hotel and neighboring storefronts establish the next development.
panels.visualGag: The small hotel conversion sets up another supposedly justified demolition of neighboring homes and shops for parking.

panels.heading: Twelve parking blocks for an L-shaped hotel
panels.description: A formula (2 x 2 x 4) - 4 = 12 overlays the corner hotel and neighboring shops.
panels.camera: Close elevated angles give way to more overhead views.
panels.action: Buildings are selected/highlighted while parking demand is calculated.
panels.visualGag: The hotel’s modest parking arithmetic sets up a much larger social price for adjacent homes and shops.
panels.notes: The four-block deduction is written on screen; the narrator explains the unoccupied quadrant of the L-shaped footprint.

panels.heading: Neighboring shops give way to asphalt
panels.description: Small neighboring buildings are removed; a paved strip is previewed across the gap behind/beside the hotel.
panels.camera: A wider demolition view gives way to close views of the pavement and lot.
panels.action: Bulldozing and pavement/stall placement replace built parcels.
panels.visualGag: The tiny luxury-conversion project spreads into surrounding parcels, repeating the garage project’s parking-first logic.

panels.heading: A loading dock is the bonus
panels.description: A fenced paved enclosure with a truck is placed beside the hotel, adjoining the surface lot.
panels.camera: Close enclosure view, rear view, then overhead lot views.
panels.action: Fence, loading-area truck prop, and parking details are placed.
panels.visualGag: The loading dock is presented as a pleasant bonus, obtained by clearing land occupied by businesses and families.
panels.notes: The truck is an editor-selected prop, not a loading demonstration.

panels.heading: The bargain: 34 spaces instead of neighbors
panels.description: Finished elevated view displays the hotel, adjacent surface lot, and fenced loading enclosure.
panels.camera: Changing views of the finished lot, with a cut to neighboring storefronts.
panels.action: Completed-lot showcase; road traffic remains visible.
panels.visualGag: Calling the lot completely worth it celebrates eighteen condo spaces and sixteen shop spaces at the narrated cost of four businesses and ten families. Parallel parkers and loading trucks become the mock villains.
panels.notes: The displacement numbers are narrated rather than written over the image.

panels.heading: The game demolition cuts to Tulsa
panels.description: After a brief replay of office-copy demolition, an aerial photograph shows wide parking lots around relatively isolated downtown buildings.
panels.camera: Hard cut from gameplay to a held aerial photograph.
panels.action: Static insert, no visible human action.
panels.notes: The presenter identifies the city as Tulsa.

panels.heading: New Haven: parking beside rail lines
panels.description: Static aerial image shows a station/rail corridor with large parking areas and surrounding development.
panels.camera: Cut to a static aerial photograph.
panels.action: Static photograph.
panels.notes: The presenter identifies New Haven, Connecticut.

panels.heading: Detroit: the actual parking landscape
panels.description: An aerial image shows a downtown grid containing large surface lots between buildings.
panels.camera: Cut to a third static aerial photograph.
panels.action: Static photograph.
panels.notes: The presenter identifies Detroit, Michigan.

panels.heading: Shoup supplies the explanatory frame
panels.description: The High Cost of Free Parking cover, naming Donald Shoup, overlays blurred/replayed parking construction.
panels.camera: Gameplay returns beneath a static book-cover overlay.
panels.action: Repeated game lot construction under the book insert.
panels.notes: The presenter draws on Shoup’s book for his parking-policy explanation.

panels.heading: The costs of free parking accumulate
panels.description: White list over gameplay: LITTLE TO NO INCOME, USES HUGE AMOUNT OF SPACE, PRODUCES STORMWATER RUNOFF, PROVIDES LITTLE TAX REVENUE, DOES NOT SERVE NON-PARKERS.
panels.camera: Changing overhead lot views beneath a fixed list that grows line by line.
panels.action: Lot-building footage repeats beneath the cost list.
panels.notes: The runoff and tax effects are part of the presenter’s argument.

panels.heading: Different uses, different mandatory spaces
panels.description: A white code-example list overlays the office lot: worker, square footage, bedroom, hospital bed, and bowling lane requirements.
panels.camera: Overhead and close oblique game views beneath accumulating white text.
panels.action: Office frontage/lot editing continues beneath captions.
panels.notes: The presenter says municipalities copy one another’s requirements instead of studying local demand.

panels.heading: The condos return as an overparking example
panels.description: The small rehab, loading enclosure, and parking strip reappear in a completed view with surrounding trucks and cars.
panels.camera: Cut back to the hotel, shown from several angles.
panels.action: Vehicles change position on surrounding roads; buildings remain fixed.
panels.visualGag: The little condo project returns with eighteen residential spaces plus commercial parking, recalling the earlier sarcastic bargain.

panels.heading: Black Friday is still mostly empty
panels.description: Dan Gilmartin’s tweet shows a mostly empty lot and says Another enormous, 3/4 empty parking lot on #BlackFridayParking. Parking minimums are killing cities.
panels.camera: Static centered tweet over moving office gameplay.
panels.action: Static tweet overlay and photograph.
panels.visualGag: Black Friday invokes peak shopping demand, but the photograph shows a mostly empty lot.
panels.notes: The tweet names @DPGilmartin and is dated 27 Nov 2015. Its occupancy claim is the author’s.

panels.heading: Parking podiums raise the cost of construction
panels.description: A low-angle photograph shows towers with tall slotted lower façades; a neighboring façade and cropped shop lettering remain in foreground.
panels.camera: Cut to a held architectural photograph, then back to gameplay.
panels.action: Static photo illustration; no character action.
panels.notes: The presenter describes the lower levels as parking podiums. The buildings and their location are unidentified.

panels.heading: Rehabs can require demolition or never happen
panels.description: The large rehab and adjoining garage return in completed neighborhood views, illustrating how a change of use alters parking obligations.
panels.camera: Game detailing gives way to changing angles and a pullback around the rehab.
panels.action: Repeated completed-site showcase and editor detailing.
panels.visualGag: The finished rehab and garage return as the presenter explains the parking obligations behind their destructive win-win story.
panels.notes: The sequence repeats the earlier garage placement; it is not another demolition.

panels.heading: Parking governs development feasibility
panels.description: Benches and planted office paths recur as the presenter discusses parking costs, skyscraper feasibility, and minimums declining since their heyday.
panels.camera: Close office views shift between the benches and roof.
panels.action: Props, plants, and benches are selected/placed.
panels.notes: The benches recall the earlier sad-lunch scene.

panels.heading: Abundant garages, scarce cheap curb spaces
panels.description: Garage placement is replayed with its neighborhood smiling icons, followed by fence/service-area detailing beside the garage.
panels.camera: Overhead and oblique neighborhood views, followed by closer garage-side views.
panels.action: Repeated garage placement/feedback is followed by adding service-space props.
panels.visualGag: The garage placement and green smiles return while the presenter describes persistent parking complaints despite abundant off-street spaces.
panels.notes: This replays the original garage story. The smiles are game feedback, not displaced residents’ opinions.

panels.heading: The burden remains while cars come everywhere
panels.description: The small hotel lot is rebuilt in reprise: pavement and parking rows appear in the cleared strip between buildings.
panels.camera: Close pavement and lot views at the small hotel, then a wider near-overhead view.
panels.action: Editor previews/places asphalt and repeated stall assets.
panels.visualGag: The heavy-vehicle refrain accompanies a replay of the hotel’s parking strip, built where neighboring buildings once stood.
panels.notes: The presenter discusses reform near transit, though no rail station appears here.

panels.heading: Improve parking in the game—and real life
panels.description: Close detailing of the hotel’s loading enclosure and surface lot leads to a wider view of the completed corner project.
panels.camera: Alternating close overhead service-area views and higher lot views.
panels.action: Props and details are adjusted around the parking/loading area.
panels.visualGag: The tutorial finishes polishing the parking spaces whose costs it has exposed, then asks viewers to reconsider parking outside the game.

panels.heading: Patron acknowledgments
panels.description: Black card reads My Patreons and lists Liam Anderson, Connie Finley, magissima, bsquicklehausen, @southhost, and Daniel Lott.
panels.camera: Hard cut to a static credit card.
panels.action: Static text; no character action.

panels.heading: One fare: channel outro
panels.description: A gray token on black reads GOOD FOR / DNE / ONE FARE beneath a translucent diagonal red stripe.
panels.camera: The credit card gives way to the token, which brightens.
panels.action: Outro emblem fades into view.
panels.notes: The fare token closes the video as a channel emblem.
